Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "The audit began on a Tuesday morning in the public services room at the Larch Street Library. We were checking the new online room-booking form with a screen reader, using the same laptop and browser that staff keep at the front desk. The library had launched the form three weeks earlier, and visitors had already used it to reserve study rooms, a small meeting space, and the recording booth. Our aim was to document how the form behaved in ordinary use, not to rate the staff who built it. We agreed to test the public page first and leave the staff dashboard for the afternoon.

Mara, the accessibility coordinator, read each step aloud while I operated the keyboard. She used NVDA with Firefox and kept the speech rate at her usual setting. We also recorded the screen and audio, after checking that the recording did not capture visitor names from the live booking system. For the test, we used a separate account created with the library’s permission. The account had no saved preferences, which helped us see what a first-time visitor would encounter. A staff member stayed nearby to answer questions about the booking rules, but did not guide us through the page.

1. The first section asked for a room, a date, and a start time. The room choices were presented as radio buttons, and NVDA announced each label and its selected state. The labels included both the room name and its capacity, such as “Quiet Room, two people.” That wording made the choices easy to distinguish. Moving through the date field was less straightforward. The field had a visible calendar button, but its accessible name was “Open.” The button worked with the keyboard, and the calendar opened, although the name did not explain what would open.

The calendar itself used a grid. NVDA announced the weekday headings, then each date, including whether it was available. Arrow keys moved between days, and pressing Enter selected one. On the first attempt, Mara moved into the next month and did not hear a clear announcement that the month had changed. She paused and checked the screen, where the month heading was visible. When she returned to the grid, she found the right date without difficulty. We noted the missing month-change announcement as a point for follow-up, rather than treating it as a failed booking.

After the date was selected, the start-time choices appeared beneath the field. They were grouped by room availability and read in chronological order. A short note above them said that reservations lasted up to two hours, but that note was not connected to the time control. Mara heard it while navigating linearly; she did not hear it when jumping directly to the form field. “I can find the options,” she said, “but I wouldn’t know the limit from here unless I read the whole page.” The note was accurate and useful, so we recorded the connection between the note and the control as the issue.

The next section collected contact details. The name and email fields had persistent labels, and the required status was announced before each field. The phone number was optional, which the page stated in visible text and which NVDA also announced. We entered a test address with a plus sign in the user name and submitted the form. It was accepted. Then we removed the final part of the email address and submitted again. The error appeared above the form and was announced as an alert. However, focus remained on the submit button, so Mara had to locate the error and then move back to the email field.

2. We checked the confirmation page after making a valid reservation. It gave the room, date, and start time in a heading followed by a short summary. The reservation number was selectable text, not an image, and NVDA read it correctly. A “Print this page” button opened the browser’s print dialog. The page also included a link to cancel the reservation, with the booking number repeated in its accessible name. We did not activate cancellation, because the test account was being used to check the confirmation flow and the library had asked us to leave valid bookings intact.

The staff member explained that visitors sometimes ask whether a confirmation has been sent by email. The page said, “A confirmation message is on its way to the address you provided.” That matched what the staff member expected, and the test inbox received the message within a minute. Its subject line included the room name and booking date. The message used a plain-text layout, and its cancellation link had descriptive text. We did not assess how the email behaved in every mail application; our checks covered the page and the test inbox available during the session.

In the afternoon, we returned to the booking form on a smaller laptop display and increased browser zoom to 200 percent. The page reflowed into one column, and the controls remained in the same logical order. The calendar required vertical scrolling, but no content overlapped. At that zoom level, a help icon beside the phone field moved below the visible area. It was decorative and did not contain instructions, so it did not prevent form completion. The text contrast was clear in the room lighting, though we did not use a color-measurement tool as part of this visit.

Before leaving, Mara reviewed the notes with the library’s web editor. They agreed on three concrete items to investigate: give the calendar button a more descriptive name, announce the calendar’s month when navigation changes it, and connect the reservation-duration note to the start-time control. They also recorded the email error’s focus behavior for review. The editor asked whether the form should be taken offline. Mara said the audit notes did not establish that it needed to be, and suggested discussing the findings with the development team. We saved the recording and test account details in the library’s restricted project folder.
